common_name: Pueblo Pecan (USDA-ARS Compact Columnar Scab-Resistant Pecan)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pueblo is a compact, columnar USDA-ARS release with early pollen shed (Type I), so pair it with a Type II pollinator such as Kanza or Oconee for a reliable crop.

directions: Pueblo pecan is the first USDA-ARS pecan release bred specifically for a compact, columnar tree form, concentrating its nut crop in the core of the canopy rather than spreading across a wide-reaching crown the way most standard pecans do, which lets it be spaced far more tightly than traditional seedling-sized cultivars. It is a cross of Osage and Creek, showing high precocity, early bud break, early pollen shed, and strong resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that drives most fungicide spraying in humid pecan-growing regions. Nuts mature early in medium clusters and shell out with big, well-filled, high-quality kernels. Because Pueblo sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive, plant a Type II (protogynous) cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, and expect the compact habit to bring trees into bearing sooner than standard full-sized pecans.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Zuni is a Pawnee x Waco cross bred for the central and western pecan-growing regions where Pawnee already performs well, and it needs a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar within range.

directions: Zuni pecan is a USDA-ARS release bred from a Pawnee x Waco cross and one of the agency's first patented pecan cultivars after decades of releasing cultivars without patent protection. It produces large nuts in medium-sized clusters with well-filled, cream-colored kernels, shows medium precocity, and carries strong resistance to pecan scab, which reduces the fungicide inputs needed in humid growing regions. Zuni is best suited to the areas where Pawnee is already a proven performer, including the central and western pecan belt, and like other pecans it needs deep, well-drained soil, consistent moisture, and a compatible pollinator planted nearby since pecans are wind-pollinated and most cultivars are not reliably self-fruitful. Trees take several years to reach bearing age and are long-lived once established.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Kalos is a University of Georgia release that needs a compatible pollinator nearby, and benefits from a regular fungicide program since its scab resistance is only moderate compared with stablemate Avalon.

directions: Kalos pecan was bred by the University of Georgia's pecan breeding program from a Sioux x Desirable cross, selected for its large nut size and high kernel percentage. The golden kernels shell out in clean, complete halves, and nuts typically mature in early fall in southern Georgia growing conditions. Kalos needs a compatible pollinating cultivar such as Elliott or Sumner planted nearby for a reliable crop. Its scab resistance is only moderate — growers in humid climates get the best results combining Kalos with a regular fungicide program, unlike its sibling release Avalon, which tolerates scab largely spray-free; plant it in deep, well-drained soil with full sun and supplemental zinc as recommended for pecans generally.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; The Beast is a vigorous 75% European/25% American hybrid released by the Hybrid Hazelnut Consortium in 2020 and is widely used as a cross-pollinating partner for Rutgers EFB-resistant cultivars such as Hunterdon, so plant it alongside a compatible companion variety rather than alone.

directions: The Beast, formally OSU 541.147, is a hybrid hazelnut bred at Oregon State and released by the Hybrid Hazelnut Consortium specifically for eastern North America, where European hazelnuts struggle against Eastern Filbert Blight. As a 75% European and 25% American hybrid it combines blight resistance inherited from the American parent 'Rush' with better nut quality and yield than typical hybrid seedling populations. It grows as a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed shrub to roughly 15-20 feet with a slightly spreading crown, bearing nuts with a kernel-to-shell ratio around 44 percent. The Beast is grown as much for its role as a compatible, cold-hardy pollinizer for Rutgers's EFB-resistant cultivars, such as Hunterdon, as for its own nut crop, so site it near a companion variety rather than as a lone planting.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Lagerstedt is a recent Oregon State University release carrying an Eastern Filbert Blight resistance gene from 'Ratoli', and it requires a compatible cross-pollinator such as Yamhill, York, McDonald, or Wepster — it is not compatible with Jefferson or PollyO.

directions: Lagerstedt is an Oregon State University hazelnut release named for retired OSU horticulture professor and USDA researcher Harry Lagerstedt. It shares a common ancestor and similar upright growth habit with the popular Jefferson release, but it carries its Eastern Filbert Blight resistance from a different source — a gene inherited from the Spanish variety 'Ratoli' on a different linkage group than the long-used Gasaway-derived resistance in earlier OSU cultivars. This matters because EFB strains that have begun overcoming Gasaway-derived resistance in some Pacific Northwest orchards are not expected to overcome Lagerstedt's distinct resistance source, giving growers an additional tool for managing blight pressure over the long term. Lagerstedt needs a compatible pollenizer planted nearby — Yamhill, York, McDonald, and Wepster are compatible, while Jefferson and PollyO are not — and otherwise follows standard hazelnut culture: well-drained, slightly acidic soil, full sun, and an upright habit that needs less structural pruning than older varieties.
sources: Oregon State University Hazelnut Breeding Program
